title: Interpolation and Numerical Differentiation
objectives: Construct the unique interpolating polynomial through a small point set and evaluate it between nodes
Explain the Runge phenomenon and why node placement or splines beat naively raising the degree
Derive forward and central difference formulas with their truncation errors
Balance truncation against rounding to choose a step size, and apply this to bump-and-revalue Greeks
motivation: You have a vol smile quoted at six strikes and need a vol at the seventh; you have a pricing library that returns prices but not derivatives, and risk needs delta and gamma *now*. Both problems extract new information from tabulated function values - and both have failure modes that can push a hedge ratio off by 50%. Interpolation and finite differences are the two tools that make tabulated data answer questions it was never asked.

blocks.text: Interpolation: one polynomial through the points

blocks.md: Given $n+1$ points with distinct $x$-coordinates, there is exactly one polynomial of degree $\le n$ passing through all of them. Uniqueness has a one-line proof: if two candidates existed, their difference would be a polynomial of degree $\le n$ with $n+1$ roots - impossible unless it is the zero polynomial. Existence and evaluation are handled by the Lagrange form or divided differences; for two or three points, direct algebra is faster than any formula.

blocks.title: Worked: the quadratic through (0,1), (1,2), (2,5)
items: Write $p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. From the first point: $c = 1$.
Now the interpolated value: $p(1.5) = 3.25$, a defensible estimate between the known points.

blocks.text: When interpolation goes wrong: Runge's warning

blocks.md: More nodes with equispaced $x$-values does **not** mean a better fit. Interpolating $f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2)$ at equispaced points on $[-1, 1]$ produces wilder and wilder oscillation near the endpoints as the degree grows - the **Runge phenomenon**. The cure is not more degree but better placement (Chebyshev nodes, clustered toward the ends) or giving up on a single polynomial: **cubic splines** stitch low-degree pieces with smooth joints and are what charting tools and curve builders actually use.

blocks.caption: The Runge function: smooth in the middle, and the place where high-degree equispaced interpolation oscillates violently near x = +/-1.

blocks.md: When $f$ is a black box - a pricing library, a simulation - you cannot differentiate symbolically. Taylor's theorem turns *evaluations* into derivative estimates. Expand $f(x+h)$:

blocks.caption: One expansion forward is enough to buy a first-derivative estimate.

blocks.title: Forward and central differences
items: **Forward**: $\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = f'(x) + \dfrac{h}{2} f''(x) + O(h^2)$ - truncation error $O(h)$.
**Central**: $\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h} = f'(x) + \dfrac{h^2}{6} f'''(x) + O(h^4)$ - truncation error $O(h^2)$, because the even-order terms cancel.
Central costs one extra evaluation and buys a whole order of accuracy - almost always worth it.

blocks.title: Worked: f(x) = x^2 at x = 3, h = 0.1
items: Forward: $(9.61 - 9)/0.1 = 6.1$. True derivative: $6$. Error $= +0.1$, exactly $\tfrac{h}{2}f'' = 0.1$ since $f'' = 2$ - the truncation term, visible in full.
Central: $(9.61 - 8.41)/0.2 = 1.2/0.2 = 6.0$ - exact, because central differences annihilate the quadratic term.

blocks.code:
f = lambda x: x * x
d = (f(3.1) - f(2.9)) / 0.2     # central difference
print(round(d, 9))              # 6.0
print((f(3.1) - f(3.0)) / 0.1)  # forward: prints 6.100000000000005-ish
print(round((f(3.1) - f(3.0)) / 0.1, 6))  # 6.1
blocks.caption: Central is exact for quadratics; forward carries the h*f''/2 term - and both carry rounding dust in the last digits.

blocks.text: The rounding floor: smaller h is not better

blocks.md: The forward error has two rivals: **truncation** $\approx \tfrac{h}{2}|f''|$ (shrinks with $h$) and **rounding** $\approx \varepsilon |f|/h$ (grows as $h$ shrinks, because dividing a tiny difference by a tiny $h$ amplifies its ulp-level noise). With $\varepsilon = 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$, the optimum sits near $h^* \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}$ for forward differences (best error ~$10^{-8}$) and near $h^* \approx \varepsilon^{1/3} \approx 10^{-5.5}$ for central differences (best error ~$10^{-11}$). Pushing $h$ to $10^{-12}$ in a double is not extra care - it is sabotage.

blocks.title: Bump-and-revalue Greeks
blocks.md: Delta: $\Delta \approx (P(S+h) - P(S-h))/(2h)$; gamma: $\Gamma \approx (P(S+h) - 2P(S) + P(S-h))/h^2$. Gamma is where desks get burned: its rounding error scales as $\varepsilon |P|/h^2$. With a \$100 option price and $h = 10^{-6}$, that is $2.2\times10^{-16} \times 100 / 10^{-12} \approx 0.02$ of pure noise - comparable to a true ATM gamma of $\varphi(d_1)/(S\sigma\sqrt{T}) \approx 0.4/20 = 0.02$. One-hundred-percent noise. A sane bump (1% of spot, or one tick) keeps truncation acceptable and the rounding floor far away.

Two modern alternatives deserve a sentence. **Automatic differentiation** propagates derivatives through code exactly (to rounding), eliminating the truncation/rounding trade-off entirely; **complex-step differentiation** $\mathrm{Im}[f(x + ih)]/h$ sidesteps cancellation for smooth functions. Production risk systems still often run bump-and-revalue, though, because it reuses the exact pricing pipeline traders trust - and because it needs no source-code access.

blocks.caption: Watch the secant through (x-h, x+h) converge on the tangent as h shrinks - and think about where rounding will bite.

blocks.md: The two topics are one idea: fit a simple object (polynomial) through known values, then interrogate it. Differentiate the interpolant and you get finite-difference formulas; the central difference is exactly the derivative of the quadratic through $(x-h, f(x-h)), (x, f(x)), (x+h, f(x+h))$. So every rule in this lesson is secretly "interpolate locally, then differentiate" - which is also why second-order accuracy is the natural default.

guidedExercise.prompt: For $P(S) = S^2$ (an illustrative pay-off-like function) at $S = 100$: (a) compute the forward first difference with $h = 0.5$ and compare with the true derivative; (b) compute gamma via the central second difference with $h = 1$ and compare with the true value.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $(100.5^2 - 100^2)/0.5 = (10100.25 - 10000)/0.5 = 200.5$ vs true $200$: error $0.5 = \tfrac{h}{2}f'' = 0.5$, the predicted truncation. (b) $(101^2 - 2 \cdot 100^2 + 99^2)/1 = (10201 - 20000 + 9801) = 2$ - exact, since second differences are exact for quadratics.

independentExercise.prompt: A vol smile is quoted at three strikes: (90, 0.22), (100, 0.18), (110, 0.16). (a) Fit the unique quadratic $q$ through the points (hint: substitute $t = x - 100$). (b) Evaluate $q$ at strike 95 and compare with linear interpolation between 90 and 100. (c) What does the sign of the quadratic coefficient tell you about the smile?
hints: With $t = x-100$: points are $(-10, 0.22), (0, 0.18), (10, 0.16)$; write $q = \alpha t^2 + \beta t + \gamma$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $\gamma = 0.18$; from $t = \pm 10$: $100\alpha - 10\beta = 0.04$ and $100\alpha + 10\beta = -0.02$; adding gives $\alpha = 0.0001$, subtracting gives $\beta = -0.003$. So $q(t) = 0.0001t^2 - 0.003t + 0.18$. (b) At strike 95, $t = -5$: $q = 0.0025 + 0.015 + 0.18 = 0.1975$ - below the linear estimate $0.20$, because the smile is flattening. (c) $\alpha > 0$: convex in strike - the smile curves upward away from the money, the signature skew-curve shape.

commonMistakes: Raising interpolation degree on equispaced nodes and trusting the endpoint wiggles - the Runge phenomenon.
Shrinking the finite-difference bump toward machine precision: rounding noise $\varepsilon|f|/h$ (and $\varepsilon|P|/h^2$ for gamma) grows faster than truncation falls.
Using forward differences where central ones cost almost nothing extra and carry one more order of accuracy.
Interpolating volatility or yields linearly in regions where the curve's curvature is the signal.
Forgetting that the central second difference is exact only for quadratics - real payoffs leave $O(h^2)$ terms.
realWorldApplication: Cubic spline interpolation is the workhorse behind curve building (yield curves, vol surfaces, image resampling), and central finite differences are the default derivative engine whenever source code is unavailable and only evaluations are possible.
quantFinanceApplication: Bump-and-revalue delta and gamma are computed exactly as in this lesson by production risk systems; the bump size is chosen to sit between truncation and the rounding floor, and vol smiles are interpolated with splines or quadratics fitted exactly as in the exercise.
summary: $n+1$ points determine a unique degree-$n$ polynomial; fit small ones by direct algebra, and beware equispaced high degrees (Runge).
Forward differences carry $O(h)$ truncation; central differences $O(h^2)$ and exactness on quadratics.
Total error trades truncation ($\downarrow h$) against rounding ($\uparrow$ as $h \to 0$): optimum $h \sim 10^{-8}$ forward, $\sim 10^{-5.5}$ central in doubles.
Gamma's rounding floor scales as $\varepsilon|P|/h^2$ - the reason production bumps are ticks or 1%, not machine epsilon.

The truncation error of the central difference $(f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h)$ is of order:
quiz.explanation: Even-order Taylor terms cancel by symmetry, leaving $\tfrac{h^2}{6}f'''$: second-order accuracy, exact for quadratics.

quiz.prompt: Why does shrinking the step $h$ below about $10^{-8}$ hurt forward-difference derivatives in double precision?
options: The function values themselves become less accurate
The rounding term $\varepsilon|f|/h$ grows as $h$ shrinks and overtakes truncation
CPUs round h itself to zero
quiz.explanation: $f(x+h)$ and $f(x)$ then differ only in their last few ulps; dividing that dust by tiny $h$ amplifies it - the rounding floor.

quiz.prompt: What exactly does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
f = lambda x: x * x
d = (f(3.1) - f(2.9)) / 0.2
print(round(d, 9))
quiz.explanation: The central difference is exact for $f(x) = x^2$; any float dust is removed by rounding to 9 places, leaving exactly 6.0.

quiz.prompt: Fit the quadratic through (90, 0.22), (100, 0.18), (110, 0.16) and evaluate it at strike 95. Answer to 4 decimals.
The standard cure for the Runge phenomenon when interpolating on an interval is:
options: double the number of equispaced nodes
use Chebyshev nodes (clustered toward the endpoints) or piecewise cubic splines
interpolate with straight lines between equispaced nodes at very high degree
quiz.explanation: Clustering nodes near the ends (Chebyshev) tames the endpoint oscillation; splines avoid a single high-degree polynomial entirely.

flashcards.back: $(f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h) = f'(x) + \tfrac{h^2}{6}f'''(x) + O(h^4)$ - second-order accurate, exact on quadratics.
High-degree interpolation on equispaced nodes oscillates wildly near interval endpoints; fix with Chebyshev nodes or splines.
